strengths: The paper addresses an important question: what multimodal contrastive learning recovers when modalities contain related, rather than identical, latent factors.

The empirical study has substantial breadth, including synthetic assumption violations, multiple CLIP backbones, distribution shifts, 11 few-shot datasets, and ground-truth factors from Multimodal3DIdent.
The proposed post-processing is inexpensive and produces promising reported improvements. For example, Table 2 increases ViT-B/16 two-shot target-average accuracy from 32.51% to 37.13%.
weaknesses: The central proof contains a fundamental error. Appendix D.1, Lemma 2 claims that the normalized contrastive loss has minimum zero and requires equal embeddings for positive pairs almost surely. Under the finite-concentration vMF model, the joint latent distribution has full support, so this equality forces constant embeddings, contradicting the required uniform outputs. Moreover, on the unit circle with k = tau = 1, identity encoders and cosine distance give approximately -0.421 in Eq. (2), disproving the claimed minimum. Both identifiability proofs rely on this lemma, leaving the main guarantees unsupported.

The convex-body proof has a separate substantive gap. Lemma 3 establishes a uniform text-latent marginal only in the limit lambda approaching zero, but Eq. (43) uses uniformity as an exact identity for Theorem 4.2. At finite lambda, a normalized truncated Laplace conditional generally produces a nonuniform marginal because its normalizer depends on location. The claimed cross-entropy equivalence and subsequent corollary therefore require revised assumptions and proofs.

The claimed ICA disentanglement guarantee is incompatible with the hypersphere assumptions. A uniformly distributed sphere-valued vector has dependent Cartesian components and no statistically distinguished orthogonal basis. FastICA cannot resolve that rotational ambiguity under Eq. (4). Adding independent components in Section 5 and Appendix O does not establish a compatible source model. The alternative PCA/local-isometry argument is also heuristic.

The downstream experiments do not isolate disentanglement as the source of improvement. Appendix K changes dimensionality across methods, and FastICA includes whitening. Dimension-matched PCA-only and whitening-only controls are essential. For fixed whitened features, an orthogonal ICA rotation leaves the optimum of an L2-regularized linear probe unchanged. Consequently, the reported accuracy gains cannot establish the claimed benefit of recovering independent components.

Direct recovery evaluation remains insufficient. CelebA relies on selected qualitative traversals and attribute counts; Appendix P reports R² without component-wise disentanglement metrics or ICA ablations. Additionally, Appendix K evaluates regression from true sources to learned features: a rank-deficient linear projection can achieve perfect R² under this protocol without preserving all latent information.

The 'beyond DAGs' contribution lacks a demonstrated causal advantage. An undirected edge specifies statistical dependence, but the paper provides neither intervention semantics nor a formal comparison with DAG models containing latent regime variables. The experiments also do not directly test mixtures of opposing causal mechanisms.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Main real-data gains lack uncertainty estimates, essential synthetic training settings and the Multimodal3DIdent protocol are underspecified, and Table 2 reports an incorrect RN101 baseline target average: the listed entries average approximately 22.03%, not 20.03%.
